chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Statistical Toolkit — Correlation, Spread, and Z-Score

lessons.title: Case Study: Calculating a Spread and Z-Score on Two NSE FMCG Stocks

children.text: This lesson runs the entire chapter's toolkit end to end on one real pair: Britannia Industries and Nestle India, two of India's most widely held FMCG staples. Both are premium, high-margin packaged foods businesses, both lean heavily on the same dealer and modern-retail distribution networks, and both get compared to each other constantly by analysts. That makes them a reasonable, realistic candidate to actually work through, correlation, spread, and z-score, rather than just describing the steps in the abstract. (All figures in this case study are illustrative.)

body.text: Running the full toolkit end to end on a real pair does two things at once: it shows you exactly how the pieces fit together, and it surfaces a genuinely important lesson this chapter has not covered yet, what to do when the number you get out looks too extreme to trust at face value.

body.caption: Twelve days of illustrative closing prices, Britannia Industries vs Nestle India

children.text: Lesson 5's rule applies immediately: screen on returns, not on these price levels.

body.code:
import pandas as pd

prices = pd.DataFrame({
    "britannia": [4950, 4980, 4960, 5010, 5040, 5020, 5070, 5100, 5080, 5130, 5160, 5220],
    "nestle":    [2330, 2345, 2328, 2360, 2372, 2358, 2385, 2400, 2390, 2415, 2428, 2405],
})

returns = prices.pct_change().dropna()
print(returns["britannia"].corr(returns["nestle"]))
# 0.604...
body.caption: Correlation computed on daily returns, not on the raw price levels above

body.label: Return correlation, Britannia vs Nestle
body.context: A moderate positive reading, not overwhelming on its own, but a reasonable starting point for two large FMCG staples with meaningfully different product mixes (biscuits and dairy vs a broader packaged foods portfolio).

children.text: Step 2: Building the Hedge Ratio Spread

A moderate correlation is enough to justify the next step, not enough to trade on. Following Lesson 6, fit a regression of Nestle's price on Britannia's, across the same twelve days, and use the residual as the spread.

body.code:
import numpy as np

x = prices["britannia"].values
y = prices["nestle"].values

beta, alpha = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
residuals = y - (alpha + beta * x)

print("beta:", round(beta, 4), "alpha:", round(alpha, 2))
print("residuals:", np.round(residuals, 2))
# beta: 0.3683  alpha: 512.73
body.caption: Fitting the hedge ratio and computing the regression residual spread

body.label: Fitted hedge ratio (β)
body.context: For every ₹1 move in Britannia, Nestle has historically moved about ₹0.37, based on this small illustrative sample, well short of the 60 to 250-plus trading days you would actually want before relying on this number.

body.title: Regression residual spread, Britannia vs Nestle (illustrative)

children.text: Step 3: Is Day 12 Actually Unusual? The Z-Score

Day 12's residual, about −₹30, is clearly the biggest move in the series just by eye. Following Lesson 7, the mean and standard deviation of the preceding eleven days turn that into a precise, standardized number.

body.code:
resid = pd.Series(residuals)  # from the regression above

mean = resid.iloc[:-1].mean()
std = resid.iloc[:-1].std()
z_today = (resid.iloc[-1] - mean) / std

print(f"mean={mean:.2f}, std={std:.2f}, z={z_today:.2f}")
# mean=2.78, std=8.05, z=-4.10
body.caption: Computing Day 12's z-score from the preceding eleven days of residual history

stats.label: Return correlation
stats.context: Moderate, a reasonable screen, not a strong signal on its own

stats.label: Day 12 residual
stats.context: Nestle underperformed its regression-predicted price by about ₹30

stats.label: Day 12 z-score
stats.context: By Lesson 7's own rough guide, beyond about 3 is rare and worth investigating, not a green light

children.text: In this illustrative scenario, Nestle India's management, on an investor call that same morning, flagged softer urban demand for packaged foods and pointed to margin pressure from higher milk solids costs. Britannia, more skewed toward biscuits and rural distribution, had no comparable commentary that day and traded broadly in line with its recent pattern. That is exactly the kind of one-sided, company-specific news Lesson 4 discussed, and it is the reason Day 12's number cannot simply be read off a chart without asking what caused it.

A z-score of roughly −4.10 looks like a screaming signal. It is also, in this case, built from a mean and standard deviation estimated using only eleven days of data, far short of the 60-plus day lookback Lesson 7 recommended. A handful of residual days, one of which happens to be an unusually large negative outlier, produces an estimate of "normal" that is itself shaky. Combine that with a genuine, specific news catalyst, softer urban demand is often a multi-quarter theme, not a one-day blip, and the honest conclusion is caution, not conviction. This is one of the more common mistakes newer stat arb practitioners make: treating a large computed number as automatically meaningful, without asking how reliably that number was actually estimated.

body.text: An extreme z-score built from a short history is not more trustworthy than a moderate z-score built from a long one. If anything, treat very large z-scores computed from small samples with extra suspicion, not extra confidence, until you have checked both the sample size and the reason behind the move.

children.text: Before this pair goes anywhere near a real trade, the twelve days used here need to become at least a year of daily data. The correlation, hedge ratio, and z-score would all get recomputed on that fuller sample, giving genuinely stable estimates instead of the illustrative, small-sample numbers in this lesson. Only after that, and after the formal cointegration test in Chapter 3 confirms the relationship is statistically real rather than assumed, does sizing an actual pairs trade, covered from Chapter 4 onward, become the next question.

body.title: Should he trade this right now?
body.scenario: A friend has seen this case study's z-score of about −4.10 and wants to immediately go long the spread, buy Nestle, sell Britannia in the fitted 0.368 ratio, betting on a sharp reversion.
body.prompt: What would you point out to him before he does this?
body.modelAnswer: Two things. First, this z-score was computed from only eleven days of history, far too short a sample for a stable, trustworthy mean and standard deviation; a genuinely reliable z-score needs a much longer lookback, ideally 60 or more trading days. Second, the move coincided with a specific, plausibly lasting piece of news, softer urban packaged foods demand and margin commentary from Nestle's own management, not an obviously random, noise-driven blip. Before trading, he should extend the price history, recompute the correlation, hedge ratio, and z-score on the fuller sample, and run the formal cointegration test from Chapter 3, rather than acting on one extreme number computed from a handful of days.

body.title: What is the biggest problem with this z-score?
body.question: In this case study, the z-score of approximately −4.10 was computed using a mean and standard deviation estimated from only eleven days of residuals. What is the main problem with treating this number as a reliable trading signal?
options: Z-scores can never be trusted, regardless of sample size
A mean and standard deviation estimated from just eleven observations are themselves unreliable, so the z-score built from them is unreliable too
The regression should have used returns instead of price levels
Nestle India and Britannia Industries are not really comparable companies
body.explanation: A z-score is only as good as the mean and standard deviation used to compute it. With just eleven days of residual history, those estimates are noisy and can be thrown off by a single unusual day, which is exactly the small-sample risk this case study is designed to illustrate. The fix is a longer lookback window, not abandoning the z-score approach altogether.

body.title: Before Trading Any Pair
steps: Compute correlation on returns, not price levels, over a meaningful sample, ideally 60 or more trading days
Fit a regression-based hedge ratio and build the residual spread, rather than relying on a naive price ratio
Compute the z-score using a sensible lookback window, not just whichever few days you happen to be looking at
If the z-score is extreme, check for real news or a structural change before assuming automatic reversion
Run a formal cointegration test (Chapter 3) before sizing any real position

points: Running the full toolkit, correlation, hedge-ratio spread, and z-score, end to end on a real pair surfaced a moderate 0.60 return correlation and an extreme Day 12 z-score of about −4.10.
An extreme z-score computed from a very short history, just eleven days here, is not automatically a trustworthy signal. Small samples produce noisy mean and standard deviation estimates.
A specific, plausibly lasting news event behind a spike, like softer urban demand commentary, is a reason for caution, not automatic confidence that the spread will revert quickly.

The correct response to an extreme, small-sample z-score is to extend the history, recompute everything on the fuller sample, and only then consider the formal cointegration test in Chapter 3, never to trade on one dramatic number alone.

This closes the loop on the chapter's toolkit: correlation screens candidates, the regression-based spread removes the naive ratio's hidden trend, and the z-score turns the spread into a comparable signal, but none of the three replaces careful judgment.
